claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by friction-induced nanocrystallization.
Severe plastic deformation produces a hard, refined tribolayer at the contact interface.
The as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating has a multiphase, relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
Increasing sliding speed or strain rate enhances friction-induced deformation.
Severe plastic deformation at the worn surface creates a nanocrystalline tribolayer.
Higher sliding speeds induce severe plastic deformation near the contact zone.
Severe plastic deformation causes rapid grain refinement near the contact zone.
The refined grain structure increases local hardness.
Increased local hardness retards wear and improves overall wear performance.
Increasing sliding speed relative to the baseline will produce a measurable nanocrystalline tribolayer at the worn surface.
Increasing sliding speed relative to the baseline will increase local hardness.
Increasing sliding speed relative to the baseline will reduce the wear rate.
At lower sliding speeds, tribolayer formation is limited and wear rates are relatively higher.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-entropy-alloy coatings under moderate loads and ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Under extreme thermal conditions, oxidation or other degradation mechanisms may dominate and limit the applicability of friction-induced nanocrystallization.
Alloy composition may affect the degree and rate of tribolayer formation.
